title: King and rook against king: fence, approach, check on the edge
outcomes: Uses the rook to fence the lone king along a file or rank from a safe distance
Brings the king up close, then finishes with a rook check on the edge that the king guards
Spots the two ways the win is thrown away: a loose rook and a stalemating quiet move
Tells positions where the method applies from positions where it does not (an extra black piece)
Explains the method to a beginner and sets up one position on a board

steps.caption: White to move, with a king and a rook against a bare king. Do not play anything yet: about how many moves of best play does it take to force mate?

claims.statement: White wins by force from here.

steps.prompt: Guess before you read on: about 3, 6, 10 or 30 moves of best play? And which piece will do more of the work, the rook or the king?

steps.text: **Mate in 10 moves.** [V: tablebase, 19 plies] Long enough that a plan beats cleverness. The rook shuts lines but cannot cover the squares next to the black king; only your king can. So the work splits into three jobs: **fence** the king in, **walk your king up** beside it, and give the **last check on the edge**. We start at the end.

steps.caption: Finish one: the kings face each other with one square between. The black king has only two moves, both along the edge.

line.say: The rook checks along the edge and also takes d8, and f8 through the king. The king on e6 covers d7, e7 and f7: no square is left.

claims.statement: Before the check the black king has only d8 and f8.
Ra8 is checkmate.

steps.caption: Finish two: in the corner. The white king stands a knight's move from the corner square.

line.say: The king on c7 covers b8 and b7. The rook check on the a-file covers a7, so the cornered king has nowhere to go.

claims.statement: Before the check the black king has only a7.
Ra1 is checkmate.

steps.caption: Finish three: the kings are two files apart on the same rank, and the black king is on the edge file. In all three finishes the black king is on the edge, White's king stands beside it, and the rook checks from far away.

line.say: The white king covers g4, g5 and g6. The rook check along the h-file closes h4 and h6. Checkmate.

claims.statement: Before the check the black king has only h4 and h6.
Rh1 is checkmate.

steps.caption: The same finish with the colours reversed. The method does not care who holds the rook.

line.say: Black's rook checks along the first rank. The king on e3 covers d2, e2 and f2. Checkmate.

claims.statement: Before the check the white king has only d1 and f1.
Ra1 is checkmate.

steps.caption: Job one: fence. The rook on a4 closes the whole fourth rank, so the black king may only stay above it. Count its squares.

claims.statement: The black king has exactly these five squares.
Black is not in check.

steps.text: **Fence from far away.** A rook shuts a whole file or rank, and the king may not cross it. Keep the rook where the king cannot reach it, or where your own king guards it. A fence must also move: slide it one line closer to the king and the area he lives in shrinks. That is the whole idea. Watch the fence move in the next three boards.

steps.caption: Fence, part one: the rook slides from file to file, and the black king is driven to the left. White wins by force in at most seven moves.

line.say: The rook closes the e-file from the far end of the board. The black king cannot cross it, and cannot attack the rook.
Black stays on the left of the fence.
The fence moves one file closer. Now the d-file is closed too, and Black has three moves, all to the left.
Black keeps going left, towards the edge.

claims.statement: The whole line is a forced mate in at most seven moves.

steps.caption: Fence, part two: now a check drives the king off the seventh rank and the white king steps up.

line.say: A check along the seventh rank from a square the king cannot reach. Black must leave that rank.
Black steps to the back rank. Ka6 was also legal; this is the engine's line.
The white king steps up. It covers b7 and c7 while the rook holds d7 and d8, so Black has one move.
Forced.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most six moves.

steps.caption: Fence, part three: the net closes in the corner. One quiet move, then the last check. Mate in at most three moves.

line.say: A check along the back rank. Only a7 is left.
Forced again.
A quiet rook move, not a check. It covers the whole back rank and leaves Black one square, a6.
The only move.
The rook checks along the a-file. The king on c6 covers b5, b6 and b7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most three moves.

steps.text: **A rule for the fence [I].** Put the rook on the file next to the black king's file, as far from the king as the board allows. When the king steps away from the fence, bring the fence one file closer. When the king comes next to the rook, move the rook away along its line. A rook left near the king is lost, as the next board shows.

steps.caption: The wrong way to fence: the rook stands next to the black king with no guard. It is Black's move.

line.say: The king takes the unguarded rook. Two bare kings are left: a draw.

claims.statement: The rook on e4 is attacked and undefended.
With Black to move, this is only a draw.

steps.text: **Job two: bring your king.** Capablanca's *Chess Fundamentals* (our notes on it) says the rook confines the enemy king to a strip, but only your own king can finish the job. With the enemy king in the centre, he advises walking your king up first, and putting it on the file next to the black king's, towards the centre, not the same file.

steps.caption: If it were Black's move here, the king would have five squares and could walk sideways. Who has the move decides what a check can do.

claims.statement: With Black to move the king has these five squares.

steps.caption: The squeeze, part one. It is White's move and the kings face each other with a gap, so the rook check cannot be answered by stepping forward. Mate in at most nine moves.

line.say: The check comes along the seventh rank from the far side. Black must go back to the last rank.
Black steps back.
The white king walks forward and takes c7, d7 and e7. Black can only slide along the last rank.
Black slides to the other side.

claims.statement: The whole line is a forced mate in at most nine moves.

steps.caption: Part two: the rook waits, the king follows, and the black king is herded toward the corner. Mate in at most seven moves.

line.say: A waiting move [I]: the rook slides along the seventh rank to a square nobody can attack, and Black has to move again.
Black moves toward the corner.
The king follows, covering d7, e7 and f7. Black has two moves, both on the back rank.
Black goes toward the corner.
The rook steps next to the black king, which is safe only because the king on e6 guards f7. Black has one move, h8.
Forced.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most seven moves.

steps.caption: Part three: the king closes in step by step, and the rook gives the last check.

line.say: The king closes in. Black has one move, g8.
Forced.
The white king takes a position facing the black king, and h8 is the only square left.
Forced.
The rook checks along the back rank. The king on g6 covers g7 and h7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: From here White mates in at most three moves.

steps.prompt: Before the next card: in the long line you just stepped through, how many of White's eight moves were checks? Write your guess.

steps.text: **Count the checks.** [V] In this line 2 of White's 8 moves are checks; the rest are quiet king steps and rook moves that keep the fence closed. [I] So the king does more of the squeezing, and the rook shuts lines. [H] Beginners overrate checks, because a check feels like progress. A check next to an unguarded rook loses it: see the contrast below.

steps.caption: A quiet rook move can be the strongest move. The white king covers e7, f7 and g7; Black has the d-file left.

line.say: No check. The rook closes the d-file from far away, and Black has exactly one move, f8.
Forced.
The rook checks along the back rank and the king on f6 covers e7, f7 and g7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: Rd1 forces mate on the next move.
White wins from here.

steps.caption: Another quiet move: the king on d6 covers c7, d7 and e7, and the rook can wait on the far side.

line.say: No check. The rook closes the b-file from far away, so Black has exactly one move, d8.
Forced.
The rook checks along the back rank, and the king on d6 covers c7, d7 and e7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: Rb4 forces mate on the next move.

steps.text: **Why it works.** [I] Mate needs an edge: a king in the middle has eight squares, on an edge five, in a corner three. The check pushes the king back only when the kings face each other with one square between **and it is White's move**. Three things break the win: a rook within the king's reach, a quiet move that leaves Black no legal move, a check when the kings do not face.

steps.caption: The kings do not face each other: the white king stands a step to the side. A check now lets the black king step forward.

line.say: The rook checks along the seventh rank from far away.
The king steps forward to f6, which the white king does not guard. The squeeze has failed, and White must begin again.

claims.statement: After Ra7+ the black king has four squares, one of them in front.
White still wins from here, but not by that check.

steps.caption: The kings face each other with a gap, but it is White's move, so a check would not help. A waiting rook move passes the turn.

line.say: A waiting move [I]: the rook stays far away, nothing is attacked, and Black must now give up the facing position.

claims.statement: Ra2 keeps the win.

steps.text: **The waiting rule [I].** Check only when the kings face each other with one square between and it is White's move. Otherwise make a safe waiting move with the rook, far from the king, and let Black come to you. The boards above are checked with the tablebase; the rule is a teaching summary, not a theorem for every position.

steps.title: A check next to the king
steps.prompt: White can also check at once with Rg8+. Predict first: does that work as well as the best move? Then find the best move.

steps.caption: A rook beside the king, with nothing guarding it, is simply lost. It is Black's move.

line.say: The black king takes the unguarded rook. Two bare kings are left, and the game is a draw.

claims.statement: The rook on d2 is attacked and undefended.
The position is a draw with Black to move.

steps.title: The rook is attacked
steps.prompt: The black king attacks the unguarded rook and it is White's move. Predict first: does the king move Kb2 keep the win as well as the best move? Then find a move that keeps the win.

steps.text: **Stalemate, the quiet disaster.** If every square is taken away but the king is not in check, the game is drawn. It happens near the end, when the king is boxed in and White plays a quiet rook move. Before any move that is not a check, count Black's legal moves. If the count is zero, find another move.

steps.caption: Two rook moves take away the king's last squares. Only one of them is mate.

line.say: The rook checks along the a-file while the king on c8 covers b8 and b7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: Before the move the black king has only a7.
Ra4 is checkmate.
The other rook move, Rg7, is only a draw.

steps.caption: The other move, Rg7: the rook takes a7 and b7, the king on c8 takes b8, and Black has no move and is not in check.

claims.statement: Black is stalemated.

steps.title: Mate or stalemate?
steps.prompt: Both Rg7 and the best move take the king's last square. Predict first: is Rg7 as good as the best move? Then find checkmate in one.

steps.text: **Three questions before every move.** One: is my rook out of the king's reach, or guarded? Two: after my move, does Black still have a legal move, or is it mate? Three: does this move take away a square or a line that Black had? [I] These questions catch the two errors this lesson showed, a lost rook and a stalemate; they do not choose the best move.

**A real ending.** From our own data (Lichess, January 2013, CC0): 180 of 121,332 games reached a bare king and rook against a king and ended in checkmate. Counting the mating side's moves from the first position with only those pieces left, the median was 15 and 82 needed more than 16 [V: counted for this lesson]. We follow a blitz game, 2163 against 1879.

**How long can it take?** [R] From any position, best play mates in at most 16 moves; I recall this and have not checked it here (our Capablanca notes flag it as an outside claim). [I] So 82 of 180 games needing more than 16 means those players, in fast games, did not take the shortest route, and still won.

steps.caption: Move 98 of the game: the rook on c8 shuts the c-file, so the black king can only use the a- and b-files. White's king is on d1.

line.say: Black's king shuffles up the b-file; the c-file stays closed.
White's king starts to walk up the d-file, two files from the black king, which cannot cross the c-file to meet it.
Black keeps to the b-file.
The white king keeps pace.
Black steps up.
The white king reaches the fourth rank.
Black steps next to the rook, which has nothing to guard it.

claims.statement: Black, to move, loses by force from here.

steps.caption: What White played at move 102: the rook goes to c3, still on the c-file, and the king keeps walking.

line.say: The rook leaves the attacked square and keeps the c-file closed.
Black has more room but cannot cross.
The white king steps up beside the fence.
Black goes back.
The king reaches the sixth rank.
Black steps up again.

claims.statement: The rook on c8 was attacked and undefended.
White's move Rc3 keeps the win.

steps.prompt: White to move, king on d6, rook on c3, Black's king on b6. If the rook now gives a check on the b-file, which squares will the black king have? Write them.

steps.caption: The finish, part one, from move 105. The rook checks from the far side of the b-file. A faster mate existed, but the game's route also wins by force.

line.say: The check cuts the king off from the b-file. It can use a5, a6 or a7.
Black picks a5.
The white king steps up and covers b5, b6 and b7. Black has two squares.
Black goes down the a-file.

claims.statement: The game's first move forces mate in at most seven moves.
A faster mate exists: Rc5 mates in at most six.
After Rb3+ the black king has three squares, all on the a-file.

steps.caption: Part two: two waiting moves with the rook, the king covers the b-file, and the last check mates. Mate in at most eight moves.

line.say: A waiting move far from the king: the b-file stays closed, and Black has two squares.
Black moves.
The king covers b4, b5 and b6. Black has a2 and a4.
Black returns.
Another waiting move, giving Black a choice between a3 and a5.
Black steps up.
The rook checks along the a-file and the king on c5 covers b4, b5 and b6. Checkmate.

claims.statement: From here White mates by force in at most eight moves.

steps.text: **Say it back.** Five rules: fence from far away; bring the king; check on the edge only when your king guards the squares; count Black's moves before a quiet move; watch the rook. Compare your explanation with this model answer, one of many: [I] 'A check only helps when the kings face each other with a gap and it is my move; otherwise I wait with the rook.' The app does not grade this: you do.
